etymology: From Old English beorcan, the sound made by a dog; appearing once in the Authorized Version as the failure of watchmen who cannot perform even this basic canine function.
biblical_def:
They are all dumb dogs, they cannot bark.

Bark appears once in the Authorized Version, in one of Isaiah's sharpest indictments of Israel's failed watchmen. The figure is deliberately humiliating: a watchdog exists for exactly one function, to raise the alarm, and the prophet's charge is that these watchmen cannot even manage that most basic act — dumb dogs, they cannot bark. The verse piles up the failure in every direction: they are blind, ignorant, sleeping, lying down, loving to slumber, a full catalogue of a watch abandoned in every particular. The word bark carries the entire weight of the accusation because it names the single thing a watchdog is for; a dog that cannot bark has failed at its whole reason for existing, regardless of any other quality it might possess. Isaiah applies the figure to Israel's spiritual leaders, whose silence in the face of approaching danger is not neutral but actively complicit — greedy dogs which can never have enough, in the following verse, each looking to his own gain rather than raising the warning their office exists to give.

The principle to recover is Isaiah's own: a watchman's silence in the face of danger is not humility or gentleness but dereliction, and the prophet reaches for the plainest possible figure — a dog too lazy even to bark — to make that dereliction impossible to excuse. Any office charged with sounding warning is judged, in this verse, by whether it makes the one sound its whole function requires.

etymology: Comparative degree of base, from Old French bas (low), appearing once in the Authorized Version to describe the disreputable men recruited to incite a riot against Paul.
biblical_def:
Certain lewd fellows of the baser sort.

Baser appears once in the Authorized Version, in the account of the riot stirred up against Paul and Silas at Thessalonica. Jealous of Paul's success in the synagogue, the unbelieving Jews took unto them certain lewd fellows of the baser sort — hired agitators recruited specifically for their willingness to make trouble, distinguished from ordinary citizens by the comparative baser, meaning lower still than an already disreputable class. The phrase names a recognizable tactic: rather than opposing the gospel through argument, its opponents assembled a mob from society's most disposable men and set the whole city in an uproar. Baser carries real moral weight in the verse — it is not a neutral social descriptor but the text's own judgment on the character of men recruited for exactly this purpose, willing to assault a private house and drag believers before the rulers on trumped-up charges of turning the world upside down. The word stands as a small but pointed observation: opposition to the gospel in Acts repeatedly finds it easier to hire a mob than to answer an argument.

etymology: From Old English bealcan, to give forth violently; appearing once in the Authorized Version as a figure for the open, contemptuous speech of the wicked.
biblical_def:
Behold, they belch out with their mouth: swords are in their lips.

Belch appears once in the Authorized Version, in a psalm of David describing enemies who return at evening, prowling the city like dogs, their mouths given to open, contemptuous speech — they belch out with their mouth. The verb pictures speech as something forced up and out involuntarily, crude and uncontrolled, the opposite of measured or careful words. David immediately supplies the deadly content beneath the crude form: swords are in their lips, so that what erupts from the mouth carries the same intent to wound as a blade, however coarse the manner of its delivery. The psalm's larger complaint is that these enemies believe themselves unaccountable — for who, say they, doth hear? — treating their belching speech as consequence-free because unseen by any watching judge. David's answer, in the verses that follow, is that the LORD does hear, and will laugh at them; the crude, careless speech that seems to escape notice is in fact fully observed and will be fully answered.

etymology: From Latin activus (active), through French activite; appearing once in the Authorized Version in the idiom 'men of activity,' meaning men of capable, energetic ability.
biblical_def:
If thou knowest any men of activity among them, then make them rulers over my cattle.

Activity appears once in the Authorized Version, in Pharaoh's instruction to Joseph concerning the settlement of Jacob's household in Goshen. The idiom men of activity does not mean busy men in the modern sense of constant motion, but capable, energetic, competent men — those fit to be entrusted with real responsibility. Pharaoh, having already granted the best of the land to Joseph's family, goes further and invites Joseph to identify from among his brothers any men of activity suitable to be made rulers over the royal cattle, a position of genuine trust in an economy where livestock represented substantial wealth. The verse is a small but telling detail in the larger narrative of Joseph's rise: the favour shown to one faithful man extends outward to create opportunity for his whole family, and it is Joseph himself, once a slave and prisoner, who is now positioned to identify and commend competence in others. Activity here names the kind of demonstrated ability that earns trust, not mere busyness.

etymology: From Latin antecessor (one who goes before), through Old French ancestre; appearing once in the Authorized Version, where forefathers is the term used everywhere else for the same idea.
biblical_def:
I will for their sakes remember the covenant of their ancestors.

Ancestors appears exactly once in the Authorized Version, closing out Leviticus's long chapter of blessings and curses with a final promise of remembrance. Where the rest of Scripture almost invariably uses fathers or forefathers for this idea, Leviticus 26:45 alone reaches for ancestors, naming the patriarchs — Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob — whose covenant the LORD binds Himself to remember even after describing, in painful detail earlier in the same chapter, the exile and scattering that Israel's unfaithfulness will bring. The single occurrence closes the chapter's movement from blessing through curse to a final mercy: I will for their sakes remember the covenant of their ancestors, whom I brought forth out of the land of Egypt in the sight of the heathen, that I might be their God. The verse ties the promise of eventual restoration not to Israel's own merit in the future but backward, to a covenant already sworn to men long dead — the ancestors' faithfulness (or rather, the LORD's faithfulness to them) becomes the ground on which their distant descendants may yet be shown mercy.

etymology: From Old French amonter (to ascend, to come up to), from mont (mountain); appearing once in the Authorized Version to state the total weight of gold overlaying the most holy place of Solomon's temple.
biblical_def:
He overlaid it with fine gold, amounting to six hundred talents.

Amounting appears once in the Authorized Version, in Chronicles' account of the building of Solomon's temple, stating the precise total weight of gold used to overlay the most holy house — six hundred talents, an enormous sum by any ancient measure. The word does the simple arithmetical work of a total, but the number it totals is itself part of the text's larger argument: Chronicles takes evident care to record exact measurements and exact quantities of costly material throughout its temple-building narrative, underscoring that the house built for the LORD's name was not built cheaply or carelessly but at a cost commensurate with the glory of the One it was built to honour. Amounting to six hundred talents stands alongside other precise figures in the same chapters — cubits of length and breadth, numbers of pillars, weights of various fittings — as part of a deliberate rhetorical strategy: extravagant, exact, verifiable cost as a form of worship in itself, offered before a single sacrifice was made within the finished house.

Precise, costly devotion is treated in this narrative as itself a form of worship, offered in materials before it is offered in sacrifice.

etymology: From Latin adjutare (to help), through Old French aider; appearing once in the Authorized Version, describing the men of Shechem who assisted Abimelech in the murder of his seventy brothers.
biblical_def:
The men of Shechem, which aided him in the killing of his brethren.

Aided appears once in the Authorized Version, in Jotham's parable-framed indictment of Abimelech's rise to power. Abimelech, Gideon's son by a concubine, had hired vain and light persons to murder his seventy half-brothers upon one stone, clearing his path to be made king at Shechem. The single occurrence of aided names precisely the men of Shechem's complicity in that atrocity — not the hand that struck the blow, but the support, funding, and cover that made the murder possible. The margin reading, Heb. strengthened his hands to kill, sharpens the sense further: this was not passive tolerance but active empowerment, hands deliberately strengthened for bloodshed. Jotham's parable, delivered from the safety of a mountaintop to the very men who had aided the massacre, pronounces a curse that both Abimelech and the Shechemites would in time devour one another — a judgment the following chapter records being fulfilled to the letter. Aided here carries the full moral weight the Authorized Version assigns to complicity: those who strengthen a murderer's hands share his guilt.

etymology: From Old French agaitier (to watch, to lie in wait), through Old North French await; appearing once in the Authorized Version as a noun naming a concealed plot against Paul's life.
biblical_def:
But their laying await was known of Saul.

Await appears once in the Authorized Version, in the account of a Jewish plot to kill the newly-converted Saul (soon to be Paul) at Damascus, later summarized in the idiom laying await. The word functions here as a noun rather than the modern verb — a laying in wait, a concealed ambush prepared in secret — and the whole force of the verse turns on the fact that this concealment failed: their laying await was known of Saul, the plot discovered before it could be sprung. The conspirators had gone so far as to watch the city gates day and night to kill him, a level of determined hostility matching the zeal Saul himself had shown only recently as a persecutor of the church, now turned against him by his former allies. The verse marks an early instance of a pattern repeated throughout Paul's ministry in Acts — plots discovered, escapes engineered, often at night and often by unlikely means (in this case, being let down the city wall in a basket) — Luke's recurring testimony that no laying await, however carefully prepared, could end the apostle's ministry before its appointed time.

etymology: From Latin augmentare (to increase), from augere (to increase); appearing once in the Authorized Version, in Moses' rebuke of the tribes of Reuben and Gad for provoking the LORD's continued anger.
biblical_def:
An increase of sinful men, to augment yet the fierce anger of the LORD toward Israel.

Augment appears once in the Authorized Version, in Moses' sharp rebuke to the tribes of Reuben and Gad, who requested to settle east of the Jordan rather than cross over with the rest of Israel to take the promised inheritance. Moses reads their request against the backdrop of the previous generation's failure at Kadesh-barnea, when the spies' evil report provoked the LORD to swear that generation would die in the wilderness rather than see the land. Now, addressing the sons of that same faithless generation, Moses charges them with rising up in your fathers' stead, an increase of sinful men, to augment yet the fierce anger of the LORD toward Israel — a warning that a new generation could repeat, and even intensify, the very unfaithfulness that had already cost their fathers forty years. Augment names the specific danger of compounding an existing provocation rather than starting fresh; Moses' fear is not that Reuben and Gad will commit some wholly new sin but that they will add to a wrath already kindled, making a bad situation worse rather than better.

The principle to recover is Moses' own diagnosis: the danger named is not merely repeating a fathers' sin but augmenting it, adding a fresh generation's provocation onto an anger already kindled by the previous one. Reuben and Gad's swift response — a binding pledge to cross over armed and fight until the conquest is complete — shows the rebuke rightly heard turns a request that could have augmented judgment into renewed covenant faithfulness instead.

etymology: From Latin affectio (a disposition, state of mind), through Old French; appearing once in the Authorized Version to describe Paul's tender desire toward the Thessalonian church.
biblical_def:
So being affectionately desirous of you, we were willing to have imparted unto you... our own souls, because ye were dear unto us.

Affectionately appears once in the Authorized Version, in Paul's tender recollection of his ministry among the Thessalonians. The word modifies desirous, together naming not a professional or dutiful concern but a warm, personal longing for the church's good. Paul immediately explains what this affectionate desire produced in practice: a willingness to have imparted not the gospel of God only, but also our own souls, because ye were dear unto us. The verse pairs doctrine and affection as inseparable in true pastoral ministry — Paul does not present his teaching as a cold transaction of information but as an act flowing from and confirmed by genuine love, comparing his care in the surrounding verses to a nursing mother cherishing her children. Affectionately here names the emotional register the Authorized Version regards as proper to gospel ministry: truth delivered is not diminished but authenticated by the depth of love with which it is delivered, and Paul offers his own remembered tenderness as the pattern other ministers of the word should follow.
webster_summary: Webster (1828), from AFFECTIONATE: full of affection; warm; tender; here as the adverb, affectionately, describing Paul's tender desire toward the Thessalonian church.
webster_full: AFFECTIONATE, adj. Having great love or affection; warmly attached.
AFFECTIONATE, adj. Proceeding from affection; tender; kind.
AFFECTIONATELY, the adverb, in warm and tender affection.
In 1 Thessalonians 2:8 the word describes Paul's desire toward the church he had planted.
The verse pairs this affection with a willingness to impart 'our own souls,' not doctrine only.
scriptures: So being affectionately desirous of you, we were willing to have imparted unto you, not the gospel of God only, but also our own souls, because ye were dear unto us.
corruption_summary: There is no live postmodern redefinition of this word; the entry exists because Paul's own pairing of sound doctrine with genuine affection stands as a corrective wherever ministry is imagined as either cold information without love or warm feeling without truth.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Affectionately retains its plain, warm sense; no rival ideology has captured the word.

The principle to recover is Paul's own model, stated plainly in this verse: gospel ministry rightly carries both content and affection together, neither substituting for the other. He does not say he imparted only doctrine, nor only feeling, but that he was affectionately desirous to impart both the gospel and his own soul — a pattern the surrounding verses ground in the tenderness of a nursing mother and the labour of a working father, both offered as models for how truth is best delivered.
roots_summary: Affectionately occurs once, in Paul's tender recollection of his ministry among the Thessalonians, naming the warm personal desire that accompanied his delivery of sound doctrine.
roots_lines: Affectionately in 1 Thessalonians 2:8 describes Paul's desire toward the church at Thessalonica.
The word is paired with a willingness to impart 'our own souls,' not doctrine alone.
The surrounding verses compare Paul's care to a nursing mother cherishing her children.
Verse 11 adds the paternal image: as a father doth his children, exhorting and comforting.
The whole chapter recalls Paul's ministry at Thessalonica as free from flattery or covetousness.
usage: Affectionately desirous of you — warm, personal longing, not mere professional concern.
We were willing to have imparted... our own souls — affection confirmed in costly action.
Because ye were dear unto us — the stated reason behind both the desire and the giving.
